Persian Wars. A series of conflicts between the expanding Persian Empire under Xerxes the First and the city-states of ancient Greece, culminating in Greek victories at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea. These wars defined Greek identity, established Greek independence from Persian domination, and catalyzed the development of Athens as a democratic superpower.

The wars began with Greek city-states in Ionia, in Asia Minor, rebelling against Persian rule around 500 BCE. Athens and other mainland Greeks supported the Ionian revolt, drawing the ire of the Persian Great King. Xerxes the First, son of Darius, mobilized an enormous army to invade mainland Greece, determined to punish Athens and expand Persian hegemony westward.

The Battle of Marathon, fought in 490 BCE before Xerxes' invasion, saw the Athenian general Miltiades achieve a stunning upset victory against a Persian expeditionary force. The victory boosted Greek confidence and demonstrated that Persian forces were not invincible. The Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE saw the Athenian navy under Themistocles destroy the Persian fleet through brilliant tactics and superior ship handling. The naval victory forced Xerxes to abandon his invasion and retreat to Asia Minor.

The Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE, the final major land engagement, saw a coalition of Greek hoplites under Pausanias decisively defeat the Persian army, effectively ending major Persian invasion attempts and confirming Greek independence. The Treaty of Callias in 449 BCE formalized peace between Athens and Persia, establishing mutual respect for spheres of influence and ending the constant warfare. This peace enabled Athens' ascendancy and the flowering of the Classical period.
